title: Cat’s Third Eyelid Showing: When It’s Normal and When It Signals Illness
description: Learn why a cat’s third eyelid may become visible, when a brief appearance can be harmless, and which accompanying signs make veterinary evaluation important.
summary: Learn why a cat’s third eyelid may become visible, when a brief appearance can be harmless, and which accompanying signs make veterinary evaluation important.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with the third eyelid partly visible while resting, shown clearly but non-graphically
content:
The third eyelid, or nictitating membrane, sits at the inner corner of the eye and normally helps protect and lubricate the cornea. A small amount may be visible while a cat is deeply asleep or just waking, but a membrane that remains raised while the cat is alert deserves context. The most important questions are whether one or both eyes are affected, whether the eye is painful, and whether the cat has other signs of illness.

Quick Answer

If this change is new, persistent, or paired with concerning symptoms, contact a veterinarian rather than assuming it is harmless. The most important warning signs for this topic include squinting, a cloudy cornea, marked redness, sudden vision change, persistent discharge, vomiting, diarrhea, appetite loss, weakness, or a third eyelid that remains visible while the cat is fully awake.

What This Sign Can Mean

Brief sleep-related visibility can be normal. Persistent elevation may occur with eye pain, inflammation, trauma, dehydration, weight loss, gastrointestinal illness, systemic disease, or nerve-related changes. A one-sided change can be more suggestive of a local eye or nerve problem, while both eyes showing may accompany a broader illness.

Why the Pattern Matters

A third eyelid that appears only for a few moments after sleep and disappears once the cat is alert is very different from a membrane that stays raised for hours. Tracking duration is often more useful than repeatedly checking the eye.

Timing, severity, and the cat’s overall condition often matter more than one isolated photograph. A mild-looking sign in a cat that is weak, not eating, breathing abnormally, or behaving neurologically abnormal deserves more attention than the same sign in a comfortable cat with a clear benign explanation.

What You Can Safely Check at Home

Observe the cat in normal room light without forcing the eyelids open. Note whether one or both membranes are visible, how much of the eye is covered, whether the cornea looks clear, and whether the cat is eating, drinking, grooming, and using the litter box normally.

Keep the observation gentle and brief. Cats in pain or distress can become defensive, and repeated manipulation can worsen an eye, ear, limb, tail, or facial problem. A short natural photo or video can be useful when the sign is intermittent, but documentation should never delay urgent care.

What Not to Do

Do not push the membrane back, touch the cornea, use human redness-relief drops, or reuse old eye medication from another pet.

Also avoid using medication prescribed for another animal, guessing a human-drug dose from the internet, or repeatedly provoking the symptom to “see if it is still there.” These actions can create new problems and can make the original condition harder to evaluate.

What the Veterinarian May Evaluate

A veterinarian may examine the cornea, pupils, tear production, eye position, and third eyelid, and may use fluorescein stain to look for corneal injury. If both eyes are involved and the cat seems unwell, hydration status, temperature, abdominal findings, and blood tests may also be considered.

The exact tests depend on the cat’s age, history, examination findings, and whether the problem looks local or systemic. Not every cat needs every test. The purpose of the examination is to narrow the possibilities safely rather than to treat the visible sign in isolation.

What to Record Before the Appointment

Write down when the problem began, whether onset was sudden or gradual, whether it is constant or intermittent, and whether it is getting better or worse. Record appetite, water intake, urination, stool, grooming, sleep, breathing, activity, and behavior. Also note recent falls, fights, outdoor access, medication changes, toxin exposure, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, or other illness signs when relevant.

For cat third eyelid showing, a concise timeline is often more useful than trying to remember every detail during the visit. If you have a photo from before the problem started, comparison can also help.

How to Decide Whether Monitoring Is Still Reasonable

Monitoring is only reasonable when the cat is comfortable, the sign is mild, there is a plausible non-urgent explanation, and no red flags are present. If the sign becomes more pronounced, lasts longer, returns repeatedly, or is joined by pain, weakness, appetite loss, breathing changes, vomiting, abnormal urination, or neurologic behavior, the situation has changed and should be reassessed.

Improvement should involve the whole cat, not only the visible sign. A swelling that looks smaller while the cat becomes lethargic is not reassuring. Likewise, a cat that becomes quieter after a painful episode may be resting, but it may also be becoming weaker.

Why Early Assessment Can Matter

Many feline problems are easier to manage when identified before the cat becomes severely ill. Cats often hide pain and weakness, so owners may underestimate the severity of a problem until appetite, mobility, or behavior changes noticeably. Prompt evaluation is especially important for eye and neurologic signs, circulation problems, inability to urinate, breathing difficulty, significant trauma, or evidence of internal bleeding.

How to Keep Your Cat Comfortable While Waiting

Use a quiet indoor room, minimize unnecessary handling, keep food, water, and the litter box easy to reach, and prevent access to stairs or high furniture if movement or balance is abnormal. Do not force food, water, exercise, or handling when the cat is distressed. For suspected trauma, keep activity controlled until a veterinarian advises otherwise.

Common Mistakes Owners Make

  • Assuming a cat is fine because it is still walking or eating.
  • Waiting for a dramatic symptom before calling.
  • Using leftover medication from a previous illness.
  • Repeatedly touching or testing a painful body part.
  • Relying on one normal behavior, such as using the litter box, to rule out serious disease.
  • Changing several things at once and making the pattern harder to interpret.

Questions Worth Asking the Veterinarian

Ask what findings make the condition urgent, what changes should trigger an immediate recheck, whether home monitoring is appropriate, and whether there are activity, feeding, or medication restrictions. If a diagnostic test is recommended, ask what question the test is intended to answer and how the result would change treatment.

Bottom Line

The safest approach is to judge the sign together with the cat’s comfort, appetite, breathing, movement, and behavior. New persistent changes or red flags deserve veterinary assessment rather than prolonged home experimentation.

A More Detailed Decision Guide

Start by asking whether the sign is truly new. Cats can have individual normal variations, but a clear change from baseline carries more information than a generic description found online. Next, decide whether the cat is comfortable and functioning normally. A cat that can rest, breathe easily, walk normally, eat, drink, urinate, and respond to the environment is different from a cat that is hiding, weak, painful, disoriented, or unable to perform a normal function.

Then consider speed. A change that develops over minutes or a few hours is usually more urgent than one that has remained unchanged for months, although chronic signs still deserve evaluation. When in doubt, calling the veterinary clinic and describing the timeline is appropriate. The clinic can help decide whether the cat should be seen immediately, the same day, or at the next available appointment. This is safer than trying to force every symptom into a single diagnosis at home.

Not every case of cat third eyelid showing requires an emergency hospital, but owners should know what changes the decision. Emergency care is appropriate when the cat cannot breathe normally, collapses, has seizures, cannot stand, cannot urinate, has a cold painful limb, shows severe uncontrolled bleeding, or deteriorates rapidly. A same-day or prompt appointment is appropriate when the cat is stable but the sign is new, persistent, painful, or unexplained. Routine monitoring is the least appropriate option when the problem is progressing or affecting basic functions.

Normal bunting is interactive and brief: the cat rubs the cheek or forehead, then moves on. Head pressing is typically more forceful, repetitive, and associated with reduced awareness or other abnormal behavior.
